Strava didn't transform running — but it proved remarkably effective at anchoring the habit for millions of practitioners, by making effort visible and social. Creative writing thrives on regularity and routine too. The question was simple: how do you transpose those mechanisms to a practice like writing?
As I built the first prototype, a second question came up: what does it mean to write in the age of LLMs? When anyone can generate text in seconds, what still makes writing valuable?
Both questions led to the same answer: practice. Writing has value because you show up and do the work. Inklyne is built on that idea.

Showing up matters more than being perfect. A few lines every day outweigh occasional marathon sessions. So: a distraction-free editor, session tracking, personal stats, and a social feed that makes your commitment visible to others.

AI is available for feedback, for structural questions, for the kind of editorial push you'd get from a thoughtful reader. But it cannot write a single line for you. The guardrails are intentional. If AI writes, we learn nothing, feel nothing.
This led to a feature I hadn't planned: session-based human authorship certification. Every session is timestamped and attributed. The act of writing becomes verifiable.

In 2021, I was working on a production Flask application when I discovered FastAPI. Type annotations on route parameters, automatic validation through Pydantic, OpenAPI documentation that writes itself. It clicked immediately.

Migrating to FastAPI didn't make sense for that project. The codebase existed, the dependencies were in place, and the churn would have been real for an uncertain gain. But the idea of annotating route handlers and letting the framework handle validation was too good to drop.
The question was obvious: can we have this on Flask?

Flask-Jeroboam is a Flask extension that brings the FastAPI developer experience to the framework. It reads type annotations on route functions, validates requests and serializes responses through Pydantic, and generates OpenAPI docs from function signatures.

The first implementation fit in ~100 lines wired into the application. Enough to validate the idea under real conditions. Late 2022, I decided to go all the way: extract it, structure it as a proper extension, write documentation, publish it.

The project stalled after that. On PyPI, but without a community to keep it alive. In February 2026, I picked it up again with a different intent. I wanted to ask a research question: can Claude contribute quality code to a project that already has five years of history, its own patterns, and decisions to respect? I'm still figuring that out.

Apicurio Registry is a schema registry rooted in the Java ecosystem. It handles schema versioning, compatibility checks, and governance. But when a Python team needs to produce or consume Kafka messages in an environment where the Java team picked Apicurio, the tooling falls short.

The first instinct is the Confluent Kafka Python client. It has SerDes built in and can talk to Apicurio in some configurations. The problem shows up when the registry uses non-default artifact group IDs. Apicurio organizes schemas into groups, a namespace concept with no Confluent equivalent. If the Java team used custom group IDs instead of
, the Confluent Python serializers can't resolve the schemas. No configuration knob, no workaround.
That's the gap. A Python team needing to work with an Apicurio registry configured by someone else, on someone else's terms, had no ready-made solution.

Apicurio-serdes is a Python library that talks to the Apicurio Registry API directly. Artifact group IDs are first-class configuration: you specify the group, the library resolves the schema, the message goes through. No need to reconfigure the registry or fork Confluent's client to patch around its assumptions.

This library was written entirely by Claude. Not scaffolded or assisted, but designed, implemented, and tested through an AI-first process. I wanted to see what OSS looks like when the code is written by an AI and the human's job is to set constraints, review decisions, and push back.

Claude Code is good at individual tasks. But once you start doing serious work, sessions that involve complex workflows, iterative planning, real artefacts, the same friction points keep appearing.

Workflows produce things: plans, drafts, designs, structured outputs. Reviewing them inline in a running conversation is awkward. You scroll, copy-paste, lose your place, then have to re-inject your decisions back into the session. There's no natural pause point.

You've built workflows that work. But remembering the exact invocation, the right command, the right context, the right flags, is its own cognitive tax every time. You spend energy on the meta-work of starting work.

Some tasks are sequential. Many aren't. But the default mode in a Claude Code session is linear. Planning what can run concurrently and what has to wait, then executing that plan without losing track, is harder than it should be.
Debussy is a meta-plugin: a plugin about using the plugin ecosystem better. It doesn't replace anything. It adds a thin layer of structure on top of whatever you're already doing with Claude Code.
The name is a small joke. Claude Debussy, the composer, was known for structure beneath apparent improvisation. That felt right.
Three things, in order of how often the friction appears:
An artefact review interface. A proper UI to review what a workflow just produced. Accept, reject, annotate, then feed the decisions back into the session.
A workflow launcher. A menu of the workflows you actually use, so launching one is a single action instead of a recall exercise.
A parallel planner. A structured way to plan a session before running it, what runs in sequence, what can be dispatched concurrently, and track execution as it happens.
A meta-plugin to supercharge the Claude Code CLI experience — review artefacts, run workflows, plan and parallelize work.

Claude Code has fundamentally changed how I work. But somewhere around week three of using it for anything non-trivial, I started noticing the same friction points appearing over and over.

The first one is review. Complex workflows produce artefacts — plans, drafts, designs, structured outputs. Reviewing them inside a running conversation is awkward. You end up scrolling, copy-pasting, losing your place. What you actually want is a proper review interface: see the thing, decide what you think, feed that decision back into the session cleanly.

The second is launching. Once you've built a few workflows, you have a collection of them. But remembering the exact invocation — the slash command, the arguments, the right context — becomes its own cognitive tax. You spend mental energy on the meta-work of starting work instead of the work itself.

The third is parallelism. Some tasks are sequential. Many aren't. But the default mode in a Claude Code session is linear: one thing, then the next. Planning a session upfront — here's what can run concurrently, here's what has to wait — and then actually executing that plan is harder than it should be.

Debussy is my attempt to fix all three. It's a meta-plugin: a plugin about using plugins better. The name is a small joke — Claude Debussy, the composer, was famous for structure beneath apparent improvisation. That felt right for a tool that adds formality to what is already a remarkably fluid experience.
It's early. The inception was last week. But the three problems it targets are real, and they compound each other. Worth building.
Claude Code is powerful out of the box. But once you start doing serious work, the gaps become visible — and fixable.
